entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during storms that lasts a few seconds and then vanishes, sometimes with a bang or leaving marks.
entries.background: Thousands of people have reported it, but there are almost no instrument recordings. No explanation is generally accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist who published Sur le tonnerre in 1837. That work introduced the term ball lightning.

entries.name: Martin A. Uman
entries.background: American lightning researcher at the University of Florida. He co-wrote a major lightning handbook with Vladimir Rakov.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who keeps a database of Russian ball lightning reports. He contributed six cases to this compilation.

entries.name: Stanley Singer
entries.background: Author of an early book on ball lightning (1971) that gathered reports from scientists.

entries.name: Stenhoff
entries.background: Author of a 1999 book on ball lightning that cites about 2400 references and discusses scientist witnesses.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: Ball lightning research is split among separate people who collect cases, build theories or run lab experiments, with little coordination.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's national network of sensors that records the time, place and strength of lightning strokes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: Germany's lightning location network, which records when and where strokes occur and how strong they are.

entries.name: positive lightning stroke
entries.background: A lightning stroke that carries positive electric charge to the ground. It is rarer than negative lightning and often has a higher peak current.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.background: Lightning that travels between a cloud and the earth, as opposed to a discharge that stays between clouds.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist who belonged to the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna. He saw a fireball in 1868 and sketched it.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen. As a child in 1951 he saw a ball break into smaller spheres that melted asphalt.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: Yale palaeontologist and president of the US National Academy of Sciences. He saw a pink fireball explode on a yacht in 1878.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German physics professor at Tübingen, famed for the 1922 experiment showing that atomic spin takes only certain values in a magnetic field.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer and later physics professor at the University of Kent. He reported a glowing sphere drifting down an airliner aisle in 1963.

entries.name: Anatoly Il'ich Nikitin
entries.background: Russian physics professor who recalled a childhood sighting and led the field investigation of the video-recorded Mitino case in Moscow in 2015.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist at the St Petersburg Academy who was killed in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity. The investigation showed ordinary lightning struck him through an ungrounded conductor.

entries.name: Frankenstein
entries.background: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel about a scientist whose experiment ends in disaster.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician who founded modern neurology and taught at Paris and the Salpêtrière Hospital. Sigmund Freud was among his students.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: Short-lived paralysis and other nerve effects caused by a lightning strike, which Charcot separated from lasting psychological after-effects.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.background: A 1936 report from Herefordshire, England, of a red-hot ball that buried itself in a tub of water and made it boil. Researchers used it to estimate how much energy a ball contains.

entries.name: Camp Blanding experiment
entries.background: Martin Uman's group triggered lightning with rockets at a Florida military base and aimed it at more than 100 ground materials. The materials produced glowing effects, but the group did not call them ball lightning.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A ball lightning recorded in 2012 by video cameras fitted with spectrum-splitting gratings in China. It showed the chemical elements in the glowing object, including iron, silicon, nitrogen and oxygen.

entries.name: Poughquag case
entries.background: A 2008 sighting at a house in Poughquag, New York, of a blue ball seen at a glass door. Later tests on the glass estimated the radiation the ball gave off.
